land.text: the Czech lands and Slovakia; the infobox's 'Proclamation 28 October 1918' and 'Czechoslovakia was founded in October 1918'

predecessors.note: Carpathian Ruthenia joined in 1919 (Carpathian Ruthenia page); the Hungarian-ruled Slovak and Ruthenian land is carried under austria-hungary here because the pages opened do not date Hungary's side.

land.text: the Czech lands: the body of the article dates the split to 31 December 1992
Slovakia: the infobox dates the dissolution to 1 January 1993

capitals.name: Prague
capitals.note: Infobox capital Prague (50 05 N 14 25 E). The government in exile sat in London from the outbreak of the Second World War ('Benes formed it in London'; the page gives no date) while Prague was the seat of the German-run Protectorate.

correction.text: Bohemia, Moravia and Slovakia at the proclamation of 28 October 1918

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's row begins in 1919, but the infobox proclamation is 28 October 1918. The page names the lands (Bohemia, Moravia, parts of Silesia, Slovakia, Carpathian Ruthenia) without dating each junction; the Czech lands and Slovakia are drawn for the first months, Ruthenia joins in 1919 (ledger).

correction.text: adds Carpathian Ruthenia: 'In April 1919, Czechoslovak control on the ground was established'

keyframe_review.note: 120,863 km2 against the infobox's 127,906 km2 (no year; ratio 0.94). The shape stops at 21.1 E and has no Carpathian Ruthenia, which the Carpathian Ruthenia page puts under Czechoslovak control in April 1919 (Saint-Germain, 10 September 1919); its 1920 successor reaches 24.7 E. The Czech-held Cieszyn Silesia is probably why Poland appears among its countries: Czechoslovak forces held the area after the fighting of 23 January 1919 until the Spa decision of 28 July 1920. The page does not say whether the far east of Slovakia (Presov region, 21.1-22.6 E) was in Czechoslovak hands in 1919; that stays as drawn in the 1920 shape.

144,816 km2 for 1920-1921 against the infobox's 127,906 km2 (ratio 1.13): Ruthenia is in, and Cieszyn Silesia is divided at Spa on 28 July 1920 ('58.1% of the area of Cieszyn Silesia, along with 67.9% of the population, was taken over by Czechoslovakia'). The pages opened are silent on Hlucin (Hultschin) and the Valtice area, which the shape may include.

145,016 km2 for 1922-1935, 1.13 times the infobox's 127,906 km2 (no year given; the infobox most likely describes the post-1945 state without Ruthenia). The 200 km2 added over 1921 are not explained by any page opened (page silent).
144,593 km2 for 1936-1937, 423 km2 less than 1935; no page opened dates a border change then (digitising difference), so the shape stands. Ratio to the infobox 1.13.

correction.text: shape unchanged but valid from October 1938 (Sudetenland), November 1938 (Vienna Award) to 14 March 1939; before October the 1936 outline stands

keyframe_review.note: 85,910 km2, below the infobox's 127,906 km2 (ratio 0.67). This is the rump after Munich (30 September 1938), the Polish annexation of Trans-Olza (2 October, 801.5 km2) and the First Vienna Award (2 November, 11,882 km2); the pages give no km2 for the Sudetenland, so the rump area cannot be checked. The shape is valid only from October 1938; January to September 1938 holds the 1937 shape. The ledger's three losses carry the step.

correction.text: the remainder of the country, occupied as the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia; the legal state continued in exile

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1939-1944: Cliopatria has no Czechoslovakia after 1938. The state was dismembered on 14-16 March 1939 (Slovakia seceded, Hungary took Carpatho-Ukraine, the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia was proclaimed on 16 March) and its government sat in exile in London. Drawn as Bohemia and Moravia, occupied (ledger occupation pair; nazi-germany carries the same occupation); the renderer may prefer to draw nothing but the hatching.

correction.text: the restored state within its 1937 borders less Carpathian Ruthenia

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1945-1946, before Cliopatria's 1947 shape: re-established 10 May 1945 (infobox); 'the Sudetenland was returned to Czechoslovakia' (Munich page); Cieszyn Silesia back to its 1920 line (Cieszyn Silesia page); Carpathian Ruthenia ceded to the USSR in June 1945 (Carpathian Ruthenia page). Same outline as the 1947 shape; the return of southern Slovakia is dated only by the 1947 Paris treaty annulment of the Vienna Award (see ledger).
129,627 km2 against the infobox's 127,906 km2 (ratio 1.01): the 1937 state less Carpathian Ruthenia (12,097 km2), ceded to the USSR in June 1945.
129,605 km2 for 1949-1952, 22 km2 less than 1948; no page dates a change (page silent). Ratio to the infobox 1.01.

129,243 km2 for 1953-1968, ratio 1.01 to the infobox; the 360 km2 difference to 1952 is unexplained (page silent). The state was 'officially' a socialist republic from 1960 and federalised in 1968-1969, with no border change.

correction.text: the 1953-1968 outline, unchanged through the federation until 1990

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1969-1990: Cliopatria has no shape between its 1968 and 1991 rows although the state continued unchanged (federalised into the Czech and Slovak Socialist Republics in 1968-1969; 'federal' name from 29 March 1990).
129,220 km2, ratio 1.01 to the infobox; Cliopatria ends in 1991 but the state dissolves on 31 December 1992 (body; the infobox says 1 January 1993).

correction.text: unchanged 1991 shape for 1992, the year of the split

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1992: the 1991 outline for the last year, to 31 December 1992.

ledger.note: 1918: Czechoslovakia is proclaimed (infobox 'Proclamation 28 October 1918'); 'Czechoslovakia was founded in October 1918', Masaryk first president from 14 November 1918. The page names Bohemia, Moravia, parts of Silesia, Slovakia and Carpathian Ruthenia as the state's lands but dates no junction.

region.text: the Cieszyn (Teschen) area, divided on 5 November 1918 by an interim agreement

ledger.note: 1919, January: fighting over Cieszyn Silesia (Teschen). The area was divided on 5 November 1918 by an interim agreement; 'on 23 January 1919 invaded the area', a battle at Skoczow 28-30 January, 'a cease-fire was signed on 3 February'. The dispute runs on until the Spa decision.

region.text: Carpathian Ruthenia (Subcarpathian Rus'), 12,097 km2 as a Czechoslovak province

ledger.note: 1919, April: Czechoslovak troops establish control in Carpathian Ruthenia. 'In April 1919, Czechoslovak control on the ground was established' after defeating local militias of the Hungarian Soviet Republic; a council of Ruthenians in the United States 'voted unanimously to accept the admission of Carpathian Ruthenia to Czechoslovakia' in May; the Treaty of Saint-Germain follows on 10 September 1919. Cliopatria draws the region only from 1920.

region.text: Cieszyn Silesia, divided along the Olza

ledger.note: 1920, 28 July: the Spa Conference divides Cieszyn Silesia. 'Eventually 58.1% of the area of Cieszyn Silesia, along with 67.9% of the population, was taken over by Czechoslovakia on 28 July 1920 by decision of the Spa Conference.' The fighting itself ended with the cease-fire of 3 February 1919.

region.text: 58.1% of the area of Cieszyn Silesia with 67.9% of the population

ledger.note: 1920, 28 July: Czechoslovakia receives 58.1% of Cieszyn Silesia (the western and southern part, including the area east of the Olza that the page calls Trans-Olza), by decision of the Spa Conference.

region.text: the Sudetenland; Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia 'lost about 38% of their combined area to Germany'

ledger.note: 1938, October: Munich. The agreement was 'reached in Munich on 30 September 1938'; the German army was to finish occupying the Sudetenland 'by 10 October'. Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia 'lost about 38% of their combined area to Germany, with some 2.8 million Germans'. The page gives no km2 for the Sudetenland.

region.text: Trans-Olza (Zaolzie), the Czech part of Cieszyn Silesia east of the Olza

ledger.note: 1938, 2 October: Poland annexes Trans-Olza after an ultimatum of 30 September: 'On 2 October, the Polish Army annexed an area of 801.5 km2 with a population of 227,399 people' (the same page elsewhere gives some 906 km2 and 250,000 inhabitants for Cesky Tesin; the Cieszyn Silesia page says 1 October).

region.text: 'the territories in southern Slovakia and southern Carpathian Ruthenia' (Kosice, Uzhhorod, Mukachevo), 11,882 km2

ledger.note: 1938, 2 November: the First Vienna Award gives Hungary southern Slovakia and southern Carpathian Ruthenia. 'The First Vienna Award was a treaty signed on 2 November 1938'; 'Czechoslovakia had to surrender the territories in southern Slovakia and southern Carpathian Ruthenia'; the Royal Hungarian Army occupied them 5-10 November (Kosice 11 November). The Munich page gives 11,882 km2; the Vienna page gives 10,390 km2 for Slovakia alone.

region.text: the Slovak State proclaimed on 14 March 1939

ledger.note: 1939, 14 March: Slovakia secedes. 'Slovak independence: 14 March 1939, when the Slovak State was proclaimed.' The Slovak State needs a dossier (slovak-republic); the south of Slovakia was already Hungarian.

region.text: the remainder of Carpathian Ruthenia (autonomous since November 1938)

ledger.note: 1939, 15-18 March: Hungary annexes Carpathian Ruthenia. Carpatho-Ukraine declared independence on 14-15 March; Hitler 'gave Hungary permission to occupy the remainder of Carpathian Rus'', and Hungary occupied it 'between March 15 and 18'.

region.text: Bohemia and Moravia, the Czech lands

ledger.note: 1939, March: Germany occupies the Czech lands and sets up the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, proclaimed on 16 March 1939 (the nazi-germany dossier dates the German entry to 15 March). The government in exile under Benes sits in London.

region.text: the Sudetenland; Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia 'lost about 38% of their combined area to Germany'

ledger.note: 1945: 'Following Allied victory and the defeat of Nazi Germany in 1945, the Sudetenland was returned to Czechoslovakia.' The page gives the year, not the month.

region.text: Trans-Olza (Zaolzie), the Czech part of Cieszyn Silesia east of the Olza

ledger.note: 1945: Trans-Olza returns to Czechoslovakia. 'On 1 September 1939 Zaolzie was annexed by Nazi Germany'; 'Immediately after the war, its borders were returned to their 1920 state.' The year is the reading of 'immediately after the war'.

region.text: Slovakia, including the district awarded to Hungary on 2 November 1938

ledger.note: 1945: Slovakia and the south of Slovakia return to the restored state. The pages opened are silent on the Slovak State's end and on when Czechoslovakia took back the district awarded to Hungary in 1938; the only dated step is the Paris Peace Treaty of 10 February 1947, which 'declared the Vienna Award null and void' (First Vienna Award page). Bridging so that the 1945 keyframe agrees with Cliopatria's 1947 shape.

region.text: Bohemia and Moravia, the Czech lands

ledger.note: 1945, May: the state is re-established. The infobox gives 'Re-establishment: 10 May 1945'; the page does not give the day the last German forces left Prague.

1945, June: Czechoslovakia cedes Carpathian Ruthenia to the Soviet Union: 'Czechoslovakia signed a treaty with the Soviet Union, officially ceding the region' (the Red Army had secured most of it by 28 October 1944). The page extract gives June 1945, no day.
1960: the state 'officially became a socialist republic', the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic; colour and dossier continue.

1968-1969: the state is federalised into the Czech Socialist Republic and the Slovak Socialist Republic; the page gives '1968-1969', the year 1969 is the researcher's choice (Cliopatria's gap begins then).
1990, 29 March: 'socialist' is dropped and 'federal' added; the state is the Czech and Slovak Federative Republic.

region.text: the whole state, 'the split formally occurred on 31 December 1992'

ledger.note: 1992, 31 December: Czechoslovakia splits into the Czech Republic and Slovakia. The body of the article says 31 December 1992; the infobox says 1 January 1993.

wars.name: Fighting over Cieszyn Silesia (Teschen)
wars.outcome: Interim division of 5 November 1918, invasion of 23 January 1919, battle at Skoczow 28-30 January, cease-fire 3 February 1919; the Spa Conference gives Czechoslovakia 58.1% of the area on 28 July 1920.
wars.note: The page does not use the name 'Seven Days' War'.

wars.name: Czechoslovak campaign against the Hungarian Soviet Republic in Carpathian Ruthenia
wars.outcome: Czechoslovak Army troops defeated local militias of the Hungarian Soviet Republic and by April 1919 'Czechoslovak control on the ground was established'.
wars.note: The page names no war; the Slovak-Hungarian War it links belongs to March 1939 (Slovak Republic).

wars.name: Dismemberment of Czechoslovakia (Munich Agreement to the occupation)
wars.outcome: Munich (30 September 1938), Polish annexation of Trans-Olza (2 October), First Vienna Award (2 November), Slovak secession (14 March 1939), Hungarian occupation of Carpathian Ruthenia (15-18 March) and the Protectorate (16 March). No war was fought by Czechoslovakia.

wars.name: World War II
wars.outcome: The Czech lands are occupied as the Protectorate until the re-establishment of 10 May 1945; the government in exile sits in London; Carpathian Ruthenia passes to the USSR in June 1945.

certainty.note: Borders were still being fixed by interim agreements and fighting (Cieszyn Silesia, Carpathian Ruthenia, Slovakia).
Treaty lines (Saint-Germain, Spa 28 July 1920); the Hlucin and Valtice adjustments are not dated by the pages opened.
Munich, the Polish annexation, the Vienna Award line and the March 1939 partition changed the lines within months; the Munich page gives areas only for Trans-Olza and the Hungarian cession.
Treaty border with the USSR from June 1945; the 1920 lines restored; no change to 1992.

notes: Page budget 5 of 5. Cliopatria Czechoslovakia 1919..1991 (9 shapes) has gaps 1939-1946 and 1969-1990, filled by new keyframes (1939 occupied Czech lands, 1945, 1969, 1992). Slovakia (Cliopatria 'Slovakia' 1992..2024) shares Q33946 with this row but is a different state: it is the successor named in identity.successors, so it keeps its own dossier. The Slovak State of 1939-1945 (slovak-republic) and the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia need dossiers from another group (nazi-germany already cites them). Not on the pages opened (page silent): the Hlucin region (1920), Valtice/Vitorazsko, the Spisz and Orava border villages, the 1919 Slovak-Hungarian line (Trianon), the day the Red Army/Czechoslovak army took Prague, Czechoslovak administration of southern Slovakia in 1945, the Bratislava bridgehead (1947). Disagreements: Trans-Olza annexed 1 October (Cieszyn page) or 2 October (Munich page); 801.5 vs 906 km2; dissolution 31 December 1992 (body) vs 1 January 1993 (infobox); Hungary's 1938 gain 11,882 km2 (Munich page) vs 10,390 km2 for Slovakia alone (Vienna page). Gazetteer names needed: Sudetenland, Cieszyn Silesia, Southern Slovakia. The extract tool returns model-written summaries: quoted phrases are the extracts' renderings.
